extracted.intended_audience: Researchers and academics who act (or may be invited to act) as peer reviewers for Elsevier journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers serving as peer reviewers of scholarly journal manuscripts, covering the purpose of peer review, the different review models (single/double/triple/open), transparency practices, sharing reviewer reports, and available training resources. Intended to help reviewers understand expectations and procedural choices used by journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers play a pivotal role in scholarly publishing. The peer review system exists to validate academic work, helps to improve the quality of published research, and increases networking possibilities within research communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elsevier relies on the peer review process to uphold the quality and validity of individual articles and the journals that publish them. Despite some limitations, the majority of the research community still believes peer review is the best form of scientific evaluation (e.g., 2015 Publishing Research Consortium survey). Use peer review primarily to validate methods/results and to help authors improve clarity, rigor and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm the journal's peer review model before reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submitting or reviewing a paper, you must therefore check which type is employed by the journal so you are aware of the respective rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different subject communities prefer different models; if unsure about the peer review model employed for a specific journal, consult the journal’s homepage or contact the editorial office directly. Knowing the model informs expectations about anonymity, report sharing, and disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single anonymized review (single-blind) — advantages and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: In this type of review, the names of the reviewers are hidden from the author. This is the traditional method of reviewing and is the most common type by far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to consider: reviewer anonymity allows for impartial decisions as reviewers will not be influenced by potential criticism from the authors. Risks/anti-patterns: authors may be concerned reviewers could delay publication to publish first; reviewers may use anonymity as justification for being unnecessarily critical or harsh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double anonymized review (double-blind) — advantages and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the reviewer and the author are anonymous in this model. Author anonymity limits reviewer bias, such as on author's gender, country of origin, academic status, or previous publication history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: articles by prestigious authors are considered based on content rather than reputation. Limitations: reviewers can often identify the author through writing style, subject matter, or self-citation — it is exceedingly difficult to guarantee total author anonymity. Elsevier provides additional double-anonymized peer review guidelines for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple anonymized review — scope and complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: With triple anonymized review, the reviewers’ identity is not made visible to the author; likewise, the author identity is not made visible to the reviewer, and neither the reviewer nor author identity is made visible to the decision-making editor (not the handling editor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handling editor (who chooses and invites reviewers) does have visibility of author and reviewer identities. The complexities involved with anonymizing articles/authors to this level are considerable, and as with other anonymized models there is still a possibility of correct identification from writing style, subject matter, citation patterns, or methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review — variants and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review is an umbrella term for models aiming at greater transparency during and after peer review. The most common definition is when both reviewer and author are known to each other during the review process. Other variants include publication of reviewers’ names on the article page, publication of peer review reports alongside the article (signed or anonymous), and publication of reports with authors’ and editors’ responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceived benefits: may prevent malicious comments, stop plagiarism, prevent reviewers from following their own agenda, and encourage open, honest reviewing. Drawbacks/anti-patterns: some see open review as less honest because politeness or fear of retribution may cause reviewers to withhold or tone down criticism. Elsevier experimented with publishing peer review reports alongside accepted papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency practices to build trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparency is the key to trust in peer review. Many journals publish additional details to promote transparency around the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of transparency practices: publishing the name of the handling editor on ScienceDirect, providing details about the number of reviewers who reviewed the article before acceptance, publishing peer review reports alongside articles (signed or anonymous), and informing reviewers about the editor’s decision and their peers’ recommendations to provide updates and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article Transfer Service — sharing reviewer comments between journals
rubrics_metrics.description: As a referee, your review report (including all comments to the author and editor) will be transferred to the destination journal, along with the manuscript, if the author agrees to transfer the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main benefit: reviewers are not asked to review the same manuscript several times for different journals. Awareness: your report will be reused by the receiving journal, so write reports with potential transfer in mind (clear, constructive, and portable feedback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make use of available training and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Elsevier offers tools and resources to help reviewers improve their reviewing skills, including Researcher Academy modules, a certified peer reviewer course, and articles on peer review innovations and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended resources listed: Researcher Academy modules, the certified peer reviewer course, articles like 'Transparency in peer review', 'Peer review using today’s technology', interviews and perspectives on publishing peer review reports. Use these to learn best practices, ethics, and evolving models of peer review.
